title: Intrahospital patient transport

sources.use: ICS Guidance on the Transfer of the Critically Ill Adult, 5th edition (22 April 2026): numbered recommendations 1-88 and Appendix 7 read in full text; UK guidance

objectives: Prepare and stabilise the patient before transfer and use the unit's checklist.
Maintain monitoring and security of patient and equipment during transfer.
Document the transfer and hand over to the receiving team.

items.text: Critically ill patients undergoing transfer are managed as critical care patients, and identical standards apply to intra- and inter-hospital transfers (ICS recommendations 1-2).

Resuscitate and stabilise the patient before transfer to reduce the physiological disturbance of movement; patients with actual or anticipated airway, ventilatory or neurological compromise should be intubated and ventilated before transfer (recommendations 58-59).
Secure the patient to the transfer trolley with a harness or belt system and stow all portable equipment securely (recommendations 77, 79).
Keep all monitors, ventilator displays and syringe drivers visible to accompanying staff and tie monitoring cables together to form an umbilicus (recommendations 74-75).
Maintain patient privacy, dignity and temperature (recommendation 66).

Staff undertaking transfers must have received specific training and competencies and must not transfer unsupervised until these are met (recommendations 24-25); a risk assessment is completed beforehand and higher-risk patients need two appropriately trained clinical escorts (recommendations 53-55).
Who may escort, the risk-assessment form and the unit's checklist are set by local policy; the guidance is UK (NHS) and is not law elsewhere.

Take a minimum of two peripheral venous or one multi-lumen central venous access; medication boluses and infusions should be available for at least twice the planned duration of transfer; with a tracheostomy, take spares in line with the National Tracheostomy Safety Project (recommendations 60-61, 65).

Use a checklist for each stage of the transfer; acute hospitals should have an organisation-wide standardised checklist for intra-hospital transfers (recommendations 69-70). The ICS example covers team, airway and breathing, circulation, neurology, GI/GU, medication, packaging, identification wristbands, monitoring and a ready-to-leave check (Appendix 7; adapted from local checklists).
Assess and document neurological status regularly (every 15 minutes for neurosciences patients, every 30-60 minutes for others) (recommendation 63).
Moving, lifting and connecting equipment, and the exact order of checks, follow the unit's transfer procedure and training.

Apply minimum standards of continuous monitoring in every intra- and inter-hospital transfer (recommendation 73); the example checklist lists ECG, SpO2 and non-invasive blood pressure for all patients and capnography, with or without invasive arterial pressure, for intubated patients (Appendix 7).

Critically ill patients are more likely to deteriorate or die during transfer than on a ward, so the guidance calls for discussing, before transfer, whether escalation of organ support is appropriate if the patient deteriorates and whether resuscitation is appropriate, and for having senior clinical input available (chapter 23, mainly written for inter-hospital transfer by ambulance; the core principle - seek senior advice early and follow the guideline/Emergency Action Cards for a deterioration or arrest - applies within the hospital too, but options such as diverting to another hospital do not).
Follow the unit's transfer escalation protocol and call for help immediately for any deterioration or arrest during an intra-hospital transfer.

Maintain a record of observations and events for every transfer and complete intra-hospital transfers in the patient's notes; copy or transmit the notes and use a transfer letter or handover document (recommendations 64, 76, 81-82).

A clinical handover must occur between referring and receiving teams, and on arrival a formal multidisciplinary handover should occur rather than separate medical and nursing conversations (recommendations 67, 84-85); keep patients and next of kin informed at every stage (recommendation 48).

checklist.text: Complete the unit's transfer risk assessment and standardised intra-hospital checklist.
Confirm the escorting team is trained, available and briefed.
Confirm the patient is resuscitated and stabilised, and that airway, ventilation and neurological compromise have been addressed before leaving.
Confirm venous access, two identification wristbands and infusions sufficient for at least twice the planned duration.
Secure the patient with the harness or belt and stow all equipment securely.
Apply the minimum continuous monitoring; keep monitors and pumps visible and tie cables together.
Record observations at the unit's interval, and assess neurological status at the guidance's intervals.
Call for help and follow the unit's transfer escalation protocol if the patient deteriorates.
Complete the transfer record and give a multidisciplinary handover on arrival.

gaps: The guidance is UK (NHS) and covers inter-hospital transfer too; the ICU nurse's role on a given unit may differ.

Chapter 23's specific content (Emergency Action Cards, ambulance-stop decisions, diversion options) is written mainly for inter-hospital transfer by ambulance; it is cited here only for the principles that generalise to intra-hospital transfer. Equipment and medication appendices and the MRI chapter: not read.
Oxygen reserve calculation (Appendix 1): not reproduced; device-specific.
The example checklist is adapted from local checklists; the unit's own checklist governs.
